voice.prosody: Hi, I'm Garret's A I assistant, presenting Windows E S Test Flow Visualization — a tool we built to understand and accelerate Windows test signal.

This started with a real conversation. A team told us that most of their R I gate tests take twelve-plus hours to run.
Instinctively, that didn't sound right — but we didn't have a clear visualization at our fingertips to show otherwise.

Three challenges. First, no visualization — we had the data and aggregate metrics, but no way to see the timeline of individual test execution relative to a build.
Second, the cause — is the bottleneck test runtime, or waiting for build artifacts?
And third, the visualization helps direct us to the long poles that impact customers most in making their code flow decisions.

With GitHub Copilot as a development partner, we had a working Gantt chart prototype in a single day.
After showing it to ES engineers, the demand was immediate — they wanted it for investigating customer builds. Within a week we stood up a shared web service.
During F H L week, we polished the experience and added dependency analysis, critical-path visualization, and rerun detection.
A I kept the focus on solving the problem, not building infrastructure.

The tool paid off immediately.
The very first time we looked at a customer branch, one testpass jumped out — a bar stretching across the entire chart, sometimes running for twenty-four hours.
It wasn't test complexity — it was a device pool capacity problem.

The fix: move those AutoPlus testpasses to a standard shared automation pool. The bottleneck disappeared.
Without the visualization, this would have stayed hidden in aggregate metrics.
Let me show you what the experience looks like for a different example. Here is the live version of our new site.
We select a branch and pick a recent build. The tool reaches out to CloudTest, T3 Nova, Media Creation and Artifact Service to assemble a complete picture of every testpass and its dependencies.

Each horizontal bar represents a testpass — when it started and ended, relative to the build. Color-coded by result.
The majority start within 16 hours of the build starting. The perception of twelve-plus hours of test execution time comes from a handful of late starting and long running testpasses — now we can ask: why did these tests start late?

Clicking a late-starting testpass shows every chunk it depends on. The red-highlighted path is the critical dependency chain.
If we produce those artifacts sooner, this entire testpass starts earlier. Multiply that across dozens of similar bottlenecks and you see how targeted improvements translate directly into faster test signal.
Try it today — pick any branch, any build, and see the full test flow story for yourself. Go to u x dot u t c t dot dev.
